A 17 éves fiú még 2022-ben érkezett Magyarországra a családjával. 2024 nyarán menedékjogot kaptak, a fiú egy budapesti iskolában folytatta a tanulmányait. Az ügyészség szerint tavaly márciusban népszerűsíteni kezdte az általa „újgenerációs tervnek” nevezett szélsőséges programot azért, hogy a környezetében élő tanulókat, oktatókat és a közösségi oldalain őt követőket megfélemlítse. Ennek részeként 2025. március 12. és április 30. között a mobiljáról nyolc budapesti iskolának, köztük a sajátjának, illetve egy oroszországi oktatási intézménynek annak hivatalos email címére küldött fenyegető üzeneteket. Ezekben egy szervezetre hivatkozva azt írta, hogy az iskolaépületekben bombákat helyeztek el, és ha nem ürítik ki az épületeket, azokat felrobbantják. A hatóságok kiürítették és átvizsgálták a megfenyegetett iskolákat, ami 300 ezer forintba került nekik. Az ügyészség 9 rendbeli terrorcselekménnyel való fenyegetéssel vádolja a fiút, és fiatalkorúak fogházában letöltendő szabadságvesztést kért rá. A fiú korábban letartóztatásban volt, jelenleg bűnügyi felügyelet alatt áll. 2025 elején sorozatos bombafenyegetések rázták meg az oktatási intézmények működését. Az egész Európát célzó fenyegetésekről ebben a cikkben írtunk bővebben. Január 23-án országszerte több mint 300 iskolában volt bombariadó, de sehol sem találtak robbanószerkezetet. A rendőrség szerint a fenyegető levelek egy helyről érkezhettek. Egy héttel később folytatódott bombariadó-hullám: aznap 44 iskola kapott fenyegetést. Ezekről kiderült, egy tiszaújvárosi fiatal küldte a leveleket, aki pár nappal korábban a saját középiskoláját is megfenyegette . https://www.dw.com/en/georgia-s-surrogac.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O7ON After Russia's invasion of Ukraine, much of the surrogacy industry shifted to Georgia Image: SWR Advertisement Three years ago, Olga, 40, and Daniel (both names changed to protect their identities) from Hamburg decided to employ the services of a surrogate mother. But surrogacy is illegal in Germany, and people whose children are born through surrogacy must pursue the legal recognition of their parenthood in German courts. Olga is a German citizen but was born and raised in Russia . That's why the couple wanted to learn more about the surrogacy market in Russia. But foreign customers have been banned from signing Russian surrogacy contracts since 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , many international agencies that liaise between surrogates and intended parents moved to Georgia . So, Olga and Daniel traveled there. Georgia new destination for surrogate mothers In recent years, Georgia, a mountainous country in the Caucasus region, has become a sort of surrogacy hub, with women traveling from all over the world to work as surrogates. According to Georgia's Public Service Development Agency, over 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in 2023 across the country. Since 2012, they've given birth to over 5,000 children. Since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine, the number of children born to surrogate mothers has skyrocketed. While an estimated 300 surrogate mothers gave birth in 2021, that number leapt to over 1,100 by 2023. Anastasia, 39, is a surrogate mother from Russia working in Georgia. She has a grown daughter and has already seen through three surrogate pregnancies. Her first was in 2021, which she used to finance a property down payment. Surrogacy in the US: a different path to parenthood To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Anastasia said she completed her first two surrogacies in Russia, and her third — for a Japanese couple, brokered through the branch office of a Moscow clinic — in Georgia. Like many surrogate mothers, she went home to Russia after the embryo was implanted and returned to Georgia when she was 22 weeks pregnant. "I live in an apartment with another surrogate mother who carried twins to term. This program was the easiest and most practical one for me, but maybe I just got lucky with the right clinic," Anastasia told DW. "Other women who gave birth in Georgia told me they had difficulties. For example, after giving birth, they had to wait a long time before they were paid." She said she's ready to become a surrogate mother again. Estimates vary, but there are about 19 clinics that offer such services across Georgia. And at around €45,000 ($50,400) to €55,000, the average service costs for agencies in the capital, Tbilisi, or Batumi, Georgia's second largest city, are only about a third of what agencies in other countries charge. Several surrogate mothers who gave birth in Georgian clinics told DW that their average salary was between €18,000 and €28,000, with premiums added for birthing twins, for example. Surrogate mothers from Ukraine in demand Daniel and Olga told DW that they spent months looking for surrogacy agency in Georgia. "Pretty soon, we had access to a list of women from Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Georgia, and were given a detailed description of the process, along with the contact information of lawyers who could help take care of the formalities," they recount. "We were a little concerned that not every agency could give clear answers about the health of some of the surrogate mothers." Both work in the medical field, and Olga said perhaps some of their questions about the physical health and possible genetic disorders might have been too probing. "We picked a 30-year-old woman from Ukraine who had already been a surrogate mother once for a European couple," she said. The Russian-Georgian agency set up half-hour long Zoom call, "but that hardly seemed enough to make a final decision," Olga added. In the spring of 2024, the couple traveled to Georgia's capital to meet Elena (her name has been changed to protect her identity). Following a long discussion, the agency had seemed reluctant when they agreed to bring her to Tbilisi for the meeting. Elena made a good first impression on the couple from Hamburg, showing them pictures of her children and telling them she wanted to use the money she earned to renovate her apartment. "They had initially told us that the surrogate would spend the entire pregnancy living in a rented apartment in Tbilisi," Olga and Daniel told DW. "But then we found out that Elena was going back home for a few months after the embryo was implanted, back to Ukraine, where there's war." Human rights experts criticize legislation Georgian laws have a weak spot, human rights lawyer Nino Bogveradze told DW: They only regulate the relationship between the surrogate mothers, the intended parents and the clinics, but they don't consider the roles that agencies play. In Georgia, surrogate mothers have limited rights. Most concerns related to their pregnancy, medical care or payment are not regulated by national law but in contracts between the parties involved. And the state does not set minimum standards for social guarantees or contractual terms. Surrogacy laws and rules vary widely across Africa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video After an embryo has been implanted, surrogate mothers are not allowed to keep the child, leave the program or end the pregnancy. Several human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the International Women's Health Coalition, say the established practice in Georgia violates women's rights to reproductive self-determination. Agencies guided by material interests "Agencies often speak of their special mission to help people have the child they've been dreaming of," Olga Doletskaya, an anthropologist studying reproduction and migration at the University of Leeds, told DW. "But in reality, they're primarily driven by financial interests. And that's why they exploit the precarious situation of surrogate mothers, and pressure intended parents." Olga and Daniel from Hamburg agree. "We were constantly being made to understand that we should decide as quickly as possible. We had to hurry because apparently several other couples were also interested in our surrogate," said Olga. And the agency kept stressing that it had paid out of pocket for bringing the potential surrogate mother to Georgia, despite that not being contractually agreed. "At some point, a representative noticed my emotional state and asked me how long I wanted to remain childless," Olga said. "I felt like I was being manipulated." The couple returned to Germany with mixed feelings and decided to shelve the idea of employing a surrogate mother — at least, for now. Mark Sheider and Oleksandr Kuntytskyi contributed to this article, which was originally published in Russian. Beállítom Madarassy Pál aranyérmet szerzett az Indiában megrendezett rejtvényfejtő-világbajnokság szenior kategóriájában – írja az MTI. A szombaton véget ért versenyen az abszolút kategóriában a japán Ken Endo győzött. A Gyimesi Péter, Gyimesi Zoltán, Madarassy Pál és Nagy Kartal összetételű magyar csapat – bár több részfordulót is megnyert – végül a negyedik helyen zárta a világbajnokságot. Egyéniben a tavalyi győztes, az angol Freddie Hand lett a második helyezett, a bronzérmet pedig a német Christian König szerezte meg. A legjobb magyar Nagy Kartal lett, aki a 11. helyen zárta a világversenyt. Civilben Nagy Kartal kutató matematikus, aki matematikatáborokat és versenyeket szokott szervezni, valamint szabadidejében szívesen bridzsezik. A szenior világbajnok Madarassy Pál, aki 2007-ben megnyerte az abszolút kategóriát is, évek óta az OLAF-ban, az Európai Csalás Elleni Hivatalban dolgozik, szabadidejében tájfut. Csapatban a japán válogatott mögött az Amerikai Egyesült Államok és az Egyesült Királyság végzett a dobogón. A versenyzők a világbajnokságon a sudoku mellett számos logikai feladvánnyal találkoztak, amik mind nyelv- és kultúrasemlegesek – derül ki a Rejtvényfejtők Országos Egyesületének a Telexhez eljuttatott közleményéből. A világbajnokságra 35 országból összesen 164 versenyző érkezett. Magyarország az első, 1992-es világverseny óta jelen van a megmérettetéseken, a Rejtvényfejtők Országos Egyesülete pedig már négyszer volt a házigazda – legutóbb tavaly, Egerben. The township laid off three police department employees, a clerical worker and a zoning employee in August. On Wednesday, those cuts faced pushback from some members of the public. Trustees discuss way forward after police layoffs In August, before the layoffs, 21 News reported that Fiscal Officer Paul Canter said the township’s police fund is projected to run a $678,538 deficit by the end of 2027. For decades, the general fund subsidized the police and zoning funds, but Canter added that rising costs and police department expansions have made the model unsustainable. Board of Trustees Chairman Eric Ungaro noted Wednesday that Poland Township has not passed a police levy since 1996. Ungaro said they have "pushed the envelope to have the best police department with the best pay.” Upon learning the department was spending more than it brought in two years ago, Ungaro said that they lost four or five officers and didn’t replace them while “getting creative” in zoning. “Could we have been better? I mean, obviously,” Ungaro said. “I know we’ve had five years’ worth of department head meetings. I’m not sure how many of them had to do with budgets.” Trustee Frank DeMain addressed public concerns about the cuts by discussing forming a police district. Though nothing is formalized, DeMain said a police district would mirror much of what the township and village have done in the Western Reserve Joint Fire District. The joint fire district serves both Poland Village and Poland Township and provides fire and EMS services. More than 60 volunteers serve as inspectors, emergency medical responders, paramedics, firefighters, and fire officers. DeMain proposed having both volunteers and elected officials serve on a police district. This would help address the police department’s current situation. “I feel horrible for the people,” Ungaro said. “We didn’t have to do what we did. We didn’t have to replace the sergeant's position; we didn’t have to hire these people and have detectives; we didn’t have to do any of it. We didn’t have to get our pay up.” He ended his time speaking on the matter by saying he has tried his best. Ungaro also said he doesn’t personally reimburse himself for money the township owes him. “Our officers now are highly paid, considering they used to be horrible,” he said. “If we only have X amount of officers and we have to live within our budget, I’m not jumping up and down to put a levy on it.” Trustees previously discussed a police levy for the November ballot, a 3-mill increase that would have brought in about $1.5 million. DeMain told 21 News in August that the township could not have met the approval deadline. Download the WFMJ app for your Apple or Android smartphone or tablet to get our push alerts as news happens. Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Abdul El-Sayed speaks to reporters in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on Sunday. Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images Michigan Analysis As Trump escalates extreme attacks, Democrats – finally – rally round El-Sayed Joseph Gedeon in Detroit Endorsement not always full-throated but party backing marks major turn after bitter split over nomination Fri 30 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 07.07 EDT Share Facing a barrage of extreme attacks from Donald Trump and his allies, the Democratic establishment is finally rallying around progressive Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s candidate in the closely watched US Senate election in Michigan. But the endorsement is not always full-throated, and often even omits his name. At a rally in Port Huron on Sunday, the US president launched the latest in a wave of Islamophobic rants against El-Sayed, erroneously branding him a “jihadist” and “Muslim Brotherhood member” while invoking 9/11. But prominent Democrats have lined up to support El-Sayed. That same weekend, the independent senator Bernie Sanders rallied with him in Grand Rapids, and former president Barack Obama stood beside him in Detroit. Days earlier, the New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez toured the state with him. This last-ditch show of solidarity marks a turn for a party that split bitterly over El-Sayed’s nomination in August, which he narrowly clinched by beating a moderate pro-Israel candidate backed by much of the central party machine. The Michigan Senate race – which could help decide which party controls the entire chamber – is close, according to polls, which have typically given El-Sayed a small lead over his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers. Senior Democrats have increasingly traveled to Michigan to back a nominee who many of the party’s leaders did not back in the primary – while making clear they are not fully aligned. In an effort to close the gap, Republicans have doubled down on their incendiary attacks. Trump has repeatedly called him “Mohammed” this month, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee has aired ads using his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants, has dismissed such attacks as a distraction. “He knows my name is Abdul. He says it every day,” he said in a statement, accusing the president of trying to “use my name and my faith to distract us” from the cost of gas, groceries and healthcare. A former Detroit and Wayne county health official, El-Sayed is running on a platform that endorses the Medicare for All proposed system of universal healthcare, and calls for taking corporate money out of politics, taxing billionaires and corporations and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He has also called for ending US military aid to Israel, while calling its war in Gaza a genocide. A Marist poll last week put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48% among likely voters. He was trailing by nearly two to one in ad spending as of early October. Obama’s Saturday appearance in Detroit was the clearest sign of the shift by the Democrat party heirarchy. He joined El-Sayed on stage on the first day of early voting – his first public show of support for El-Sayed since the August primary – while a protest held by the white nationalist and 6 January rioter Jake Lang took place outside. The former president likened the attacks on El-Sayed’s name to those he faced himself. “I remind them his name was Barack,” El-Sayed said. Obama, whose 57% favorable rating in a CNN poll conducted in May is the highest of any living president, also rejected the idea that El-Sayed is radical. “What is so radical about wanting everybody to have healthcare?” he asked, saying El-Sayed would “finish the job we started” with the Affordable Care Act. But Obama acknowledged that he did not agree with El-Sayed, who has criticized some of his decisions as president, all the time. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.” Both Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders have transferred $1m to the El-Sayed campaign. Former vice-president Kamala Harris appeared with him in Detroit last month. Senator Elissa Slotkin, who spoke at the same rally, told the crowd she was counting on El-Sayed as a partner in confronting Trump’s agenda in Congress. Yet she has also said she and El-Sayed “don’t agree on everything — and that’s OK”, and previously argued that condemning the leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, with whom El-Sayed has campaigned , should not be hard. Others have been more guarded. The Senate Democratic leader,Chuck Schumer, who has now endorsed El-Sayed, said his views on Israel were “much different than mine”, while the former congressman Sander Levin endorsed him despite what he called “significant disagreement” on the same subject. Representative Hillary Scholten said she would not campaign with anyone who associates with Piker. Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey, who has historically been pro-Israel, gave a similarly noncommittal answer on CNN on Wednesday, when anchor Boris Sanchez played a clip of a Black pastor saying some voters fear that El-Sayed would prioritize issues abroad such as Gaza over Michigan’s needs. Booker spoke about his family roots in Michigan and about “winning back the Senate” without mentioning El-Sayed by name. When Sanchez pointed out to him this was not “a ringing endorsement”, Booker remained stone-faced, and the segment continued. But the coolest response came from Haley Stevens, the pro-Israel congresswoman El-Sayed beat in August by less than a point. She had been backed by groups including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) , which spent close to $30m backing her – the lobby’s largest investment in a single race. Asked by CNN’s Dana Bash on Sunday whether she was still fully behind him, she said she was “on the team”. “You didn’t mention Abdul El-Sayed in that last answer,” Bash noted. Stevens replied that she had urged El-Sayed to give a speech addressing Black voters’ concerns, and that it had not happened. In the primary, Stevens beat El-Sayed in Wayne county, home to majority-Black Detroit, taking about 51% of the Democratic vote to his 45%. Obama urged Saturday’s crowd to back the full ticket. El-Sayed and Stevens are set to campaign together on Sunday – two days before election day – it emerged last night, in what would be their first joint public appearance in months. Rogers, meanwhile, is courting Jewish voters, traditionally more likely to back Democrats, by telling the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that El-Sayed is “anti-Jew”, a charge El-Sayed rejects. Whether a cautious and caveated embrace by the Democratic establishment is enough for El-Sayed will be settled on Tuesday, in a state Trump won by less than two points in 2024. If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim US senator. To get there, he has already pulled a skeptical party machine toward his side.
